frameworks.name: Free Training Project Model
frameworks.definition: A pre-launch proof-accumulation strategy where the founder delivers full service in exchange for a charitable donation (not payment to themselves) and a testimonial/before-after right, building social proof without the awkwardness of early selling.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi, before launching his paid fitness coaching business in 2013, ran a project he called the Free Training Project in which clients donated $500-$1,000 to a charity of their choice instead of paying him, in exchange for his coaching and the right to use their before-and-after photos. After roughly one year, he had approximately 10-12 strong testimonials, which he then used to transition those same clients to a paid arrangement by framing it as donating to the charity of Alex.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Pre-revenue stage with no existing social proof
Founder has genuine prior expertise the market already informally requests
Service business where result documentation (before/after) is feasible
claims.mechanism: Charitable framing removes the psychological friction of early selling for both founder and client; the client perceives value (write-off, goodwill) and agrees to testimonial rights, so the founder accumulates proof assets without the awkwardness of asking strangers to pay for unproven work.

numbers.axis: Donation amount per Free Training Project client

bounded_by: Requires the founder to already have latent demand (people asking for the service as a favor)
Does not apply when no result documentation is possible

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that what people ask you to do for them as a favor is a leading indicator of what you can charge for later, because it signals genuine demand that has already cleared the social proof bar without payment friction.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Pre-revenue stage
Skill is one that others already request informally
claims.mechanism: Unpaid requests reveal that perceived value exceeds the social cost of asking, which is a lower bar than monetary willingness-to-pay but a reliable directional signal for viable service offerings.
bounded_by: Does not apply if requests come only from close friends who would ask regardless of skill level

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the minimum viable infrastructure to start a service business is a bank account and a payment processor, nothing else. He points to approximately 30 million existing US businesses as evidence that the setup problem is tractable for anyone capable of running a business.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business (not product requiring inventory or physical location)
Early stage before regulatory or insurance requirements force additional overhead

numbers.axis: Number of US businesses that have solved the setup problem

bounded_by: Does not apply to businesses requiring licenses, physical storefronts, or upfront inventory

claims.text: Alex Hormozi ran an online fitness coaching business in 2013 generating $4,000 per month in revenue (20 clients at $200/month) while spending only four hours every Saturday on fulfillment, demonstrating that a founder's hourly rate on a simple online service can far exceed what they earn at a job.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Online one-on-one coaching with standardized deliverables (updated training programs, macros, meal plans)
Small client base (20 clients) where personal text-based communication was sufficient

numbers.axis: Revenue and time cost of Alex Hormozi's 2013 online coaching business

bounded_by: Hormozi notes he hated the repetitive nature of the work and chose not to scale it further, so this specific model is not presented as an ideal path

claims.text: Alex Hormozi chose to transition from paying charity to paying himself by telling existing Free Training Project clients the exact same amount they had donated to charity could now go to the same cause — Alex himself — because, as he framed it, Alex cannot eat either. A portion of those clients accepted the framing and became paying customers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Client already experienced and valued the service
Client already made a charitable donation in the same dollar range
Founder frames the ask using humor and self-deprecation rather than a sales pitch
claims.mechanism: Reframing the existing donation behavior as now benefiting the founder removes the novelty of paying; the client has already committed the same dollar amount voluntarily, so the psychological barrier to repeating it toward the founder is lower than a cold price introduction.
bounded_by: Only applicable after a client has already received real value and made the prior charitable payment

claims.text: Alex Hormozi selected the gym business over a test prep company and a frozen yogurt franchise primarily because startup capital constraints eliminated the higher-potential options: the yogurt business required $250,000 (which he did not have), and a partnership miscommunication ended the test prep plan, leaving fitness as the only remaining viable option given his $50,000-$60,000 in savings.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder has limited personal savings (~$50,000-$60,000)
Multiple business ideas under consideration simultaneously

numbers.axis: Startup capital required vs available for Alex Hormozi's three 2013 business ideas

bounded_by: Hormozi explicitly states the test prep business was probably the smarter choice and he regrets not pursuing it
Selection was driven by elimination, not strategic ranking

claims.text: Alex Hormozi cold-contacted approximately 40 gym owners offering to work for free as an apprentice; only one responded. That owner ran a mastermind, which Hormozi joined for $10,000 despite not yet owning a gym, reasoning that learning from the mistakes of current gym owners before starting would be worth the cost.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Pre-launch stage with capital available but no industry contacts
Skill gap in operational and business knowledge of the target industry

numbers.axis: Alex Hormozi's 2013 apprentice outreach and education spend

anchors.region: mastermind investment before owning a gym

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's rationale for joining a mastermind before owning a gym was that he could learn from the mistakes of existing gym owners before making them himself, converting others' tuition (paid in errors) into his own knowledge at a fixed dollar cost rather than a time-and-money cost.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Mastermind members are operating businesses in the exact domain the founder intends to enter
Founder has capital to invest in education before generating revenue
claims.mechanism: Observing others' operational mistakes pre-launch is less expensive than making the same mistakes yourself, because mastermind tuition is a one-time fixed cost whereas business errors compound (lost clients, sunk time, reputation damage).
bounded_by: Value depends on whether mastermind members are far enough ahead to have made instructive mistakes

claims.text: Alex Hormozi, while working as an apprentice for a gym owner, chose to earn the learning rather than the income: he lived on approximately $400 per month in rent (splitting a bedroom) and roughly $100 per week on food, making his $50,000 in savings sufficient for at least two years of runway, so he could prioritize skill acquisition over earnings.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder has meaningful savings providing runway
Founder is early in career with no dependents or fixed obligations
Learning is the primary goal of the current role, not income maximization
claims.mechanism: Compressing personal expenses to near zero converts saved capital into time — each dollar not spent on lifestyle extends the runway during which the founder can prioritize skill acquisition over earnings, compounding the eventual earning rate once skills are deployed.

numbers.axis: Alex Hormozi's monthly personal living costs during 2013-2014 apprentice period

anchors.region: savings runway at this burn rate

bounded_by: Requires no dependents and no fixed high obligations
Hormozi explicitly notes he was 23 at the time — framing this as a life-stage-specific trade

claims.text: Alex Hormozi's apprentice employer quickly reversed the unpaid arrangement and paid him minimum wage (~$2,800/month), yet Hormozi continued to earn more from his four-hour Saturday online coaching business ($4,000/month) than from the full-time apprenticeship, confirming that the purpose of the apprenticeship was to learn, not to earn.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder has a parallel income source covering living expenses
Primary job is chosen for learning access, not compensation

numbers.axis: Monthly income from two concurrent activities for Alex Hormozi, 2013-2014

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the point of early-stage work for a future entrepreneur is to learn, not to earn, and that having a financial runway (savings) is the mechanism that makes this trade rational — without runway, the founder is forced to optimize for income rather than skill accumulation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder is pre-launch, identifying the industry they intend to operate in
Founder has savings runway of at least 12-24 months
claims.mechanism: When financial pressure is absent, the founder can choose roles and contexts that maximize learning speed rather than wage; skill compounding from this phase yields a much higher eventual return than incremental wage accumulation would.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the founder has fixed financial obligations that cannot be deferred

claims.text: Alex Hormozi describes his decision to start a gym instead of scaling his profitable online coaching business as irrational in retrospect: the online business cost four hours per week and produced $4,000/month, yet he chose not to scale it because he disliked the repetitive work. He acknowledges that the wiser decision would have been scaling what was already profitable.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Hormozi's stated motivation for the gym was legitimacy — he did not consider online coaching a real business in 2013

claims.text: Alex Hormozi transitioned his Free Training Project clients from a charity-donation arrangement to a direct-payment arrangement by asking: are you comfortable paying the same amount you were donating to charity — except now the charity is me, because Alex cannot eat either. He reports that a meaningful fraction of those clients agreed and became his first paying customers, from whom he then solicited referrals.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Client had already paid a comparable amount (to charity) and received the service
Client had already agreed to testimonial/documentation rights as part of original deal
claims.mechanism: Prior charitable behavior at the same dollar amount creates a precedent for willingness-to-pay; the client's reference point is already set at that price, so the ask feels like substituting recipient rather than accepting a new cost.

examples.text: When Hormozi was deciding between three business ideas in 2013 — a test prep company, a frozen yogurt franchise, and a fitness business — capital availability was the decisive filter. The yogurt franchise required $250,000 to start; he had $50,000-$60,000 saved. The test prep company collapsed when the professor partner he recruited either misunderstood or appropriated the materials Hormozi had prepared. That left fitness as the only option with both personal competence and no capital barrier to entry. He had been obsessed with training since age 15, had competed in powerlifting with several state records by age 23, and already had strangers asking him for workout programs as favors — all signals of latent demand.

After accumulating 10-12 strong before-and-after results through the Free Training Project, Hormozi made a public post in 2013 announcing he had built a website and was open for business. He included testimonials and a link to the site. From that post, he attracted approximately 20 men interested in physique-focused training (bodybuilding/powerlifting-adjacent). He charged each $200/month, which produced $4,000/month in revenue. Fulfillment took four hours every Saturday: updating training programs, macros, and meal plans, and sending them via text. Every client had his personal cell number for questions.

After the online coaching business was running, Hormozi cold-emailed approximately 40 gym owners asking if he could apprentice for free. One responded. That owner ran a mastermind for gym operators. Hormozi paid $10,000 to join the mastermind even though he did not yet own a gym, reasoning that he could learn from the mistakes of the existing members before making them himself. The mastermind owner initially questioned whether it made sense for Hormozi to join without a gym; Hormozi argued it did, because observing others' errors pre-launch is more efficient than experiencing them personally. The owner eventually hired Hormozi as an employee, paying him roughly minimum wage (~$2,800/month).

practices.text: To get your first paying clients when you have no social proof: offer the service for free or in exchange for a charitable donation (at the price you intend to charge later), require the client to let you document their results, and accumulate 10-15 strong before-and-after cases before transitioning to paid.
When starting a service business, identify what people already ask you to do as a favor — that informal demand is the signal of what you can later charge for.

When building toward a business, minimize personal living expenses to the point where your savings give you at least 12-24 months of runway, freeing you to prioritize learning over income during the skill-accumulation phase.
Before launching in an industry, cold-contact operators in that industry offering to work for free or cheap; use the access to learn the operational mistakes others have already made and paid for.

When transitioning a client from free or charity-based service to paid, frame the ask as the same dollar amount going to a different recipient — not as a new expense — to preserve the price reference point already established.
